'''''Eucalyptus woodwardii''''', commonly known as '''lemon-flowered gum''' and also '''Woodward's blackbutt''',<ref>Chippendale, G.M. (1973) ''Eucalypts of the Western Australian goldfields (and the adjacent wheatbelt)'', Canberra. AGPS  p.143</ref> is a small tree or mallee that is endemic to Western Australia. The [[Noongar]] name for the tree is '''Gungurra'''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|title=Noongar names for plants|access-date=6 December 2016|publisher=kippleonline.net|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170802081508/http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|archive-date=2 August 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Description==
The tree typically grows to a height of {{convert|6|to|15|m|ft|0}}<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus woodwardii''|id=5799}}</ref> and a canopy that spreads to over {{convert|3|m|ft|0}}.<ref name=seed>{{cite web|url=https://australianseed.com/shop/item/eucalyptus-woodwardii|title=''Eucalyptus woodwardii''|access-date=14 November 2017|publisher=Australian Seed}}</ref> It has smooth, white, pink, greenish or light copper coloured bark that sheds in ribbons. [[Juvenile (organism)|Juvenile]] leaves are stalked, ovate to broad-lanceolate to elliptical, to 18 x 9 cm. Adult leaves have a disjunct arrangement and are stalked. The leaf blade has a broad-[[lanceolate]] shape, basally tapered and are about {{convert|18|cm|in|0}} in length and {{convert|5|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide. Leaves are dull, grey-green to glaucous and concolorous.<ref name=nsw>{{cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/euctax.pl?/PlantNet/Euc=&name=Eucalyptus+woodwardii|title=Eucalyptus woodwardii|work=Eucalink|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Sydney|access-date=14 November 2017}}</ref> Lemon yellow flowers appear in late winter to late spring. Each axillary, simple conflorescence has three to seven flowered umbellasters on terete peduncles. The buds have a  rostrate or urceolate appearance with a calyx calyptrate that sheds early. The [[fruit]] is bell or urceolate shaped that are about {{convert|1.5|cm|in|2|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.4|cm|in|2|abbr=on}} wide. Fruits have depressed discs and enclosed valves and contain red coloured seeds that are linear and cuboid.<ref name=nsw/><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus woodwardii'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_woodwardii.htm |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=27 May 2020}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus woodwardii'' was first formally described in 1910 by the [[botanist]] [[Joseph Maiden]] in the ''[[Royal Society of Western Australia|Journal and proceedings of the Natural History and Science Society of Western Australia]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus woodwardii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455402|publisher=APNI|access-date=22 January 2020}}</ref><ref name="Maiden">{{cite journal |last1=Maiden |first1=Joseph |title=On two new Western Australian species of ''Eucalyptus'' |journal=Journal and Proceedings of the Natural History and Science Society of Western Australia |date=1910 |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=42–44 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/52468089#page/50/mode/1up |access-date=22 January 2020}}</ref> The [[Type (biology)|type]] specimens were collected by the surveyor [[Henry Deane (engineer)|Henry Deane]] in 1909 from along the [[Trans-Australian Railway]] line about {{convert|120|mi|km|0}} east of [[Kalgoorlie, Western Australia|Kalgoorlie]].<ref name="Maiden" />

==Distribution==
Lemon-flowered gum is found on flats and rises with a field distribution that is limited to east of [[Kalgoorlie]] in [[Western Australia]] in the Karonie area, and with sand or deep sandy loam.

==Cultivation==
The tree is a very popular ornamental in southern Australia due to its attractive, large, lemon-yellow flowers.<ref>Brooker, I. & Kleinig, D.,(1996) ''Eucalyptus, An illustrated guide to identification'', Melbourne. Reed Books.</ref> The cascades of yellow flowers, grey weeping foliage makes the drought tolerant tree suitable for many gardens. It is also frost tolerant and attracts bees and birds. Used as a privacy screening plant or a feature plant it has a medium growth rate and requires little pruning.<ref name=out>{{cite web|url=https://www.australianoutbackplants.com/our-plant-list/eucalyptus-woodwardii-lemon-flowered-gum|title=Eucalyptus woodwardii - Lemon Flowered Gum|publisher=Australian Outback Plantation|access-date=14 November 2017}}</ref> It is commercially available in seed or as [[tubestock]].<ref name=out/><ref name=seed/>

In the 1970s hybrids between this and coral gum (''[[Eucalyptus torquata|E. torquata]]'') called ''Torwood'' had been developed.<ref>Chippendale, G.M. (1973) ''Eucalypts of the Western Australian goldfields (and the adjacent wheatbelt)'', Canberra. AGPS  p.144</ref>
